newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan sees progress in Russia defence chief visit.
newsitem.headline: Japan sees progress in Russia defence chief visit.

text.p: Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov on Sunday wrapped up a landmark Japan visit in which he promised troop cuts and expanded defence exchanges with Tokyo and gave Moscow's blessing to closer U.S.-Japan military ties.

Rodionov's visit, the first by a Russian defence chief, sidestepped a thorny dispute over Russian-held islands north of Japan but was welcomed as a sign of warming ties between two neighbours who have fought four wars this century.
"With this, I feel we have finally made a step forward," Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told reporters on Sunday. "Now it is important to see how we can build a close relationship with Russia."

In a statement Japanese officials said would have been unthinkable during the Cold War, Rodionov told his Japanese counterpart, Fumio Kyuma, that Moscow welcomed efforts to strengthen the U.S.-Japan military alliance.
"We do not hold concerns about the U.S.-Japan military alliance and understand it is not directed against any third country," Japanese officials quoted Rodionov as telling Kyuma on Saturday.

"We welcome that Japan and the United States are building even closer security ties," Rodionov said in reference to a review of U.S.-Japan military cooperation under the 1960 U.S.-Japan Security Treaty to be completed by November.

Rodionov suggested holding tripartite military exercises between Russia, Japan and the United States as a way to establish military cooperation among the three countries in the Asia-Pacific region, a Russian defence ministry official told Russia's Itar-Tass news agency in Tokyo.
Tass quoted the Russian official as saying that Kyuma had replied that the suggestion "required study".
Rodionov told Kyuma his government had pledged a reduction of 200,000 troops this year, following cuts of 1.5 million troops since the end of the Soviet Union.
Rodionov did not elaborate but Japanese officials said they expected some of the troop reductions would be in the Far East.
The Russian troop cut plans did not include forces in the disputed islands called the Southern Kuriles by Moscow and the Northern Territories by Japan, the officials said.
The islands, which lie northeast of Japan's northernmost main island Hokkaido, were seized by Soviet troops at the end of World War Two and heavily fortified during the Cold War.

Russia and Japan fought two full-fledged wars this century, the 1904-1905 Russo-Japanese War and World War Two, as well as two other undeclared wars -- Japan's 1918-1922 Siberian Intervention and a clash in 1939 along the border between Mongolia and Japan-held northeastern China.
In 1993, Russian President Boris Yeltsin, on a visit to Tokyo, agreed to settle the dispute through political dialogue.
The islands were not on the agenda for Rodionov's Tokyo visit, but Hashimoto said he hoped the improved security atmosphere would lead to a resolution of the dispute.

The visit by Rodionov, who held talks with Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda on Friday and reviewed Japan's navy fleet at Yokosuka naval base, follows the first visit by a Japanese defence minister to Moscow last year.

The two sides also agreed to start or expand on a wide variety of defence exchanges, including mutual visits by the head of the chiefs of military staff, defence researchers, military academy cadets, obervers to war games and fleets.

In the first such port call to Japan since the 19th century, Russia will send a navy cruiser to Tokyo next month in response to a visit to Vladivostok by the Japanese cruiser Kurama last year, sent to celebrate the 300th anniversary of the birth of Peter the Great's Russian navy.
